shipped_row.boundary_rationale: The row opens at web:Ps.109.6 where an unmarked singular “him” replaces the plural accusers of the preceding row—הַפְקֵ֣ד עָלָ֣יו רָשָׁ֑ע (web:Ps.109.6 = oshb:Ps.109.6, “Set a wicked man over him”)—and no reported-speech verb (a 'saying' or 'who say' construction) introduces the shift; on the frame bytes this reads as the psalmist continuing his own prayer against a singular, representative adversary rather than resuming a quotation of the accusers’ own words. A jussive curse-chain runs unbroken through the span, opening יִֽהְיֽוּ (oshb:Ps.109.8) and bounded by a fatherless-root inclusio: בָנָ֥יו יְתוֹמִ֑ים (web:Ps.109.9 = oshb:Ps.109.9, “his children be fatherless”) and, echoing it, ח֝וֹנֵ֗ן לִיתוֹמָֽיו (web:Ps.109.12 = oshb:Ps.109.12, “no one to extend kindness...to have pity on his fatherless children”)—two distinct fatherless-root spellings, swept separately: 109:9's spelling recurs in 3 verses book-wide (2 outside this span); 109:12's spelling is unique to 109:12 book-wide (1 verse), inside this span. The unit closes on יְהִֽי אַחֲרִית֥וֹ לְהַכְרִ֑ית (web:Ps.109.13 = oshb:Ps.109.13, “Let his posterity be cut off”).
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: A minority reading takes web:Ps.109.6-Ps.109.19 as the psalmist quoting the very curse his accusers pronounced against him—resuming, after the intervening description, the reported speech flagged by web:Ps.109.2’s “They have spoken to me with a lying tongue” so that the singular “him” is the psalmist himself. The Hebrew supplies no quotation-opening verb at the web:Ps.109.5|Ps.109.6 seam to settle the question, so this rival is a live, byte-honest alternative, not excluded by the frame.

A shared remembrance-root binds oshb:Ps.109.14-Ps.109.16: the verb opening יִזָּכֵ֤ר עֲוֺ֣ן אֲ֭בֹתָיו recurs as the noun זִכְרָֽם (web:Ps.109.15 = oshb:Ps.109.15, “their memory”) and again in the motive clause יַ֗עַן אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹ֥א זָכַר֮ (web:Ps.109.16 = oshb:Ps.109.16, “because he didn’t remember”). The curse then resumes as a clothing image: וַיֶּאֱהַ֣ב קְ֭לָלָה (web:Ps.109.17 = oshb:Ps.109.17, “he loved cursing”) and וַיִּלְבַּ֥שׁ קְלָלָ֗ה (web:Ps.109.18 = oshb:Ps.109.18, “He clothed himself also with cursing”)—the cursing-noun shared by both verses is otherwise unattested in the book (sweep: 2 of 2 skeleton hits book-wide, both here). shipped_row.boundary_rationale: Three vocatives receive a shared two-part formula (3 times) in turn -- an imperative to trust in Yahweh (singular at 115:9, plural at 115:10-11) followed by the closing clause “He is their help and their shield” -- which alone is byte-identical across all 3 verses -- addressed to Israel (יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל (oshb:Ps.115.9), web:Ps.115.9), the house of Aaron (בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10), web:Ps.115.10), and those who fear Yahweh (יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11), web:Ps.115.11); the closing refrain (עֶזְרָ֖ם וּמָגִנָּ֣ם הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.115.9)) is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) across all 3 verses. The same three-member roster recurs at web:Ps.118.2-Ps.118.4 with a jussive 'let…say' verb replacing the imperative; the fixed collocation בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10) sweeps to 4 verses book-wide and יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11) to 6 verses book-wide, both concentrated in this recurring triad (Ps 135:19-Ps 135:20, outside this span, inserts a fourth member, house of Levi, before repeating the fearers clause).
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv9-11 as three separate one-verse rows would split one triadic (3-member) refrain unit whose members share one closing clause verbatim (byte tier, 3 verses).

prev_row.boundary_rationale: The idol polemic runs as one catalogue: idols are מַ֝עֲשֵׂ֗ה יְדֵ֣י אָדָֽם (oshb:Ps.115.4) ('the work of men's hands') with mouths that don't speak, eyes that don't see, ears that don't hear, noses that don't smell, hands that don't feel, and feet that don't walk (web:Ps.115.5-7), before the maker/trust indictment closes it, “Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them” (web:Ps.115.8). The catalogue's cola (e.g. פֶּֽה לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ עֵינַ֥יִם לָ֝הֶ֗ם וְלֹ֣א יִרְאֽוּ (oshb:Ps.115.5)) share one noun-then-negated-verb syntax across web:Ps.115.5-7 through 115:7's first two cola ("their hands, they don't feel" / "their feet, they don't walk"); the pattern breaks at 115:7's own third colon ("nor do they speak through their throat," negative-verb-first with no leading body-part noun) -- the catalogue still runs as one unbroken unit through the seam at 8|9, just not on a fully uniform syntax; the closing verb כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.8) ('everyone who trusts in them') catches on the imperative יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בְּטַ֣ח (oshb:Ps.115.9) ('Israel, trust!') that opens the next strophe, marking the seam at 8|9.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the sense-organ catalogue (vv5-7) from its opening (v4) and closing indictment (v8) would fragment one anaphoric list across three rows with no independent tier-1 seam between them.
observed_substrate_signals: the 3 sense-organ cola of web:Ps.115.5-7 pair a body-part noun with a negated verb apiece, e.g. אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ אַ֥ף לָ֝הֶ֗ם וְלֹ֣א יְרִיחֽוּן (oshb:Ps.115.6), in the same pattern (sweep: 3 verses)

web:Ps.115.8's closing root (כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.8), 'everyone who trusts in them') recurs as the imperative opening web:Ps.115.9 (יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בְּטַ֣ח (oshb:Ps.115.9), 'Israel, trust!')
prev_row.device_notes: The maker/trust catchword bridges idols and Yahweh across the row seam at 8|9: the psalm's argument turns on the same root used initially for misplaced trust, then for rightly placed trust.

next_row.boundary_rationale: The verb יְבָ֫רֵ֥ךְ (oshb:Ps.115.12) ('he will bless') repeats across a second, narrated triad -- “He will bless the house of Israel. He will bless the house of Aaron” (web:Ps.115.12), “He will bless those who fear Yahweh, both small and great” (web:Ps.115.13) -- before the strophe widens into a direct blessing on the congregation, “May Yahweh increase you more and more” (web:Ps.115.14) and “Blessed are you by Yahweh, who made heaven and earth” (web:Ps.115.15). The root behind יְ֭בָרֵךְ (oshb:Ps.115.13) occurs 4 finite times across web:Ps.115.12-13 alone, mirroring the trust-triad's three-member roster in narrated rather than imperative form before the address widens at v14.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the narrated bless-triad (vv12-13) from the widened blessing that follows (vv14-15) is a genuine rival: 115:14 shifts to 2mp address ('increase you', x2) and 115:15 opens with the 2mp independent pronoun 'you' -- a real addressee-register change at 13|14, not the absence an earlier reading of this seam claimed. The row nonetheless keeps 12-15 together because the 'bless' root (oshb:Ps.115.12 x3, oshb:Ps.115.13 x1) that opens the narrated triad reappears at oshb:Ps.115.15's 'blessed are you,' framing the whole span as one blessing-movement from narration to direct declaration; the seam is live, and this reading is held at medium confidence.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: A reflective aside on the affliction just survived -- “I believed, therefore I said, "I was greatly afflicted."” (web:Ps.116.10) and “I said in my haste, "All people are liars."” (web:Ps.116.11) -- leads into the pivotal question that launches the vow movement, “What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?” (web:Ps.116.12).
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching v12's question to the following cup-of-salvation verse (v13) as its answer is defensible, but the question itself closes the reflective aside begun at v10 and is the strophe's rhetorical hinge rather than the start of the vow's content.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.10-11 (הֶ֭אֱמַנְתִּי כִּ֣י אֲדַבֵּ֑ר אֲ֝נִ֗י עָנִ֥יתִי מְאֹֽד (oshb:Ps.116.10) … אֲ֭נִי אָמַ֣רְתִּי בְחָפְזִ֑י כָּֽל הָאָדָ֥ם כֹּזֵֽב (oshb:Ps.116.11)) is a well-known crux in Hebrew syntax -- the exact logical relation between 'I believed' and the quoted self-report is debated among translations -- a content difficulty distinct from the row's boundary, which rests on the aside's self-contained question-and-answer shape

web:Ps.116.12's question מָֽה אָשִׁ֥יב (oshb:Ps.116.12) ('what will I give') has no grammatical antecedent in vv10-11, which themselves carry no divine-name token at all -- the same feature that makes v13's answer ('I will take the cup...') a live continuation; the row keeps v12 with the aside because its interrogative form, not its content, closes the self-contained question-and-answer shape of vv10-12 rather than opening the vow's declarative content
shipped_row.device_notes: The reflective aside (vv10-11) is the psalm's hinge between the deliverance report and the vow movement that the question of v12 opens.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: Yahweh's character is stated generally -- “Yahweh is gracious and righteous… Yahweh preserves the simple” (web:Ps.116.5-6) -- before the speaker addresses their own soul, שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי (oshb:Ps.116.7) (“Return to your rest, my soul,” web:Ps.116.7), reports the deliverance in three parts, “my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling” (web:Ps.116.8), and resolves to “walk before Yahweh in the land of the living” (web:Ps.116.9).
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v7 (self-address alone) would separate the resolve 'return to your rest' from the report of deliverance it anticipates in v8.

prev_row.device_notes: The soul-address device (v7) frames this row's report of deliverance, resolving into the resolve-to-walk clause of v9.

next_row.boundary_rationale: The opening vow half-strophe begins, כּוֹס יְשׁוּע֥וֹת (oshb:Ps.116.13) (“I will take the cup of salvation,” web:Ps.116.13), closing on וּבְשֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֶקְרָֽא (oshb:Ps.116.13) ('and call on Yahweh's name') then the vow-payment formula (web:Ps.116.14); an interlude on death's value follows, “Precious in Yahweh's sight is the death of his saints” (web:Ps.116.15), and the speaker names themself “your servant, the son of your servant girl” (עַ֭בְדְּךָ בֶּן אֲמָתֶ֑ךָ, oshb:Ps.116.16, web:Ps.116.16), immediately followed by “You have freed me from my chains” (פִּ֝תַּ֗חְתָּ לְמוֹסֵרָֽי, oshb:Ps.116.16, web:Ps.116.16).
